Lamborghini Miura Turns 60, No Better Way To Celebrate Than This $9,900 Limited Edition Pen
19 photos
Photo: Montegrappa
The pen is mightier than the sword. But is it mightier than the original Supercar, the Lamborghini Miura, in building an owner the aura of refinement, superiority, elegance, luxury, and class? Montegrappa thinks it is.
A pen is a very discreet personal item - more elusive than a wristwatch, less conspicuous than cufflinks, and less used than a necktie stickpin. And yet, it holds more power than any other item in the world. It makes words into law, it shapes destinies more than all of humanity's arsenals, and it has power over time itself - it writes both history and the future. And it does all that with something as simple as a signature.
But simple it is not, as Giuseppe Aquila, owner and CEO of Montegrappa, gracefully explained for us in an interview. So, what's the story about the Miura? Glad you asked. Read on and learn how a writing instruments company put pen to paper (literally and metaphorically), and crafted one of the most beautiful homages to one of the most beautiful and emblematic (Lamborghini) cars ever made.
When the Lamborghini Miura debuted at the Geneva Motor Show in March 1966, its racing-derived transverse mid-engine layout did not just revolutionize motoring, it single-handedly invented the supercar. Now celebrating its 60th anniversary in October 2026, the Sant'Agata Bolognese icon is being immortalized by Montegrappa. "We're very proud of this collaboration because personally Miura for me is one of the best cars ever produced," Aquila told Autoevolution during our conversation.
Photo: Montegrappa Why pair a legendary Italian supercar with a traditional ink instrument in our heavily digitized modern era? Because a bespoke pen commands a presence that rivals any exotic machine parked outside. "In our case, first of all, our pens are not just simply writing instruments," Aquila explained. "They are a status symbol, they are accessories, like a fashion accessory, and the fountain pen is also an item linked to culture".
While smartphones handle daily notes, luxury pens seal life's biggest milestones. "You use the pen to sign an important contract, you use a pen to sign when you're getting married, maybe when you're getting divorced, you use it when you buy a house," Aquila noted. Furthermore, a Montegrappa study conducted with a neuroscientist proved handwriting engages the amygdala and long-term memory, helping students perform two times better than digital typists.
That tangible connection between mechanics and emotion unites Bassano del Grappa with Sant'Agata Bolognese. "This is not our first collaboration with Lamborghini, so we are licensees of Lamborghini for writing instruments," Aquila said, recalling their first five-color series launched two years ago for the automaker's 60th anniversary.
Photo: Montegrappa In October 2026, Montegrappa releases two new collections before Christmas, namely the accessible open-edition Lamborghini Icon and the flagship Automobili Lamborghini Miura.
To craft the Automobili Lamborghini Miura pen, Montegrappa's designers closely studied the original Bertone-styled supercar. "We only make 60 pieces of each version, so it means 60 pieces yellow, 60 pieces green, 60 pieces black, of either the fountain pen version and the rollerball version," Aquila explained. Selected by Automobili Lamborghini from 1966 best-sellers, the 3 shades, Giallo Fly, Verde Miura, and Black, apply genuine car paint onto aluminum barrels.
Every millimeter of the silhouette reinterprets the Miura's unmistakable proportions, crowned by a miniature pop-up headlamp on the cap. "This headlamp, you could actually tilt it forward, you can open and move forward, right? So even the pen has a similar mechanism," Aquila beamed. "There's a special mechanism, a push-pull: you push and it comes out, and then you can press it in and it will click back into position".
Photo: Montegrappa "The headlamp itself is made of rock crystal, and the surface underneath the rock crystal is actually engraved with the same pattern, the same texture as the lamp itself," Aquila added. Other cues abound: the barrel end mirrors the rear Venetian louvres, the serial number sits on a honeycomb grille, the cap band echoes the side vents, the clip mimics the hood slats, and the wood-and-leather box replicates the seats.
Uncapping the fountain pen reveals an 18-karat gold nib electroplated in black ruthenium, stamped with the Automobili Lamborghini shield, offered in four iridium-tipped grades, and paired with Austrian ink and a CNC-turned vulcanized ebonite feeder. Unlike ABS plastic, ebonite retains memory. "Older cars like Miura, you needed some mileage to get the best, rodaggio we call it in Italian (editor’s note: break-in ), " Aquila compared, noting the feeder adapts to pressure over a period of two weeks.
Engineering this mechanical jewel stretched from early 2025 to October 2026. "Normally a project like this, from the idea to the actual introduction of the product into the market, requires from a minimum of one year to two years," the writing instruments supremo explained. Following one to two months of research and one month of Lamborghini design feedback, prototyping takes up to three months plus a couple more for final factory approval.
Photo: Montegrappa Once approved, Montegrappa builds a pre-series batch for brutal durability trials. "There is a drop test, so the pen is dropped from 120 cm on the floor and we see how it reacts," Aquila revealed. Beyond that 47.2-inch drop, pens are cycled in a climatic chamber from -4°F to 122°F (-20°C to +50°C) at 0% to 100% humidity, tested against human sweat, and tumbled with sharp metal keys.
Founded in 1912 as Elmo ahead of Tibaldi in 1916, Aurora in 1918, and Omas in 1921, Montegrappa operated uninterrupted through both World Wars and once employed 400 workers producing pens for Waterman and Sheaffer. After pioneering limited editions in 1992 and regaining family independence from Richemont, Aquila's 60 artisans cut annual output from 100,000 pens to below 50,000, including under 5,000 collector pieces that generate 50% of total sales.
Photo: Montegrappa Among those 60 specialists are hand-engravers, stone setters, and a trio of miniature painters, led by a master who, after having spent 26 years restoring Renaissance paintings in Valencia, Spain, needed six months to master curved barrels, and trained an apprentice for four years. Although fountain pens generate 60% of Montegrappa's revenue and rollerballs and ballpoints take 20% each, "with the Lamborghini pens, we sell more rollerballs than fountain pens, " Montegrappa’s boss observed.
Priced at 8,250 euros ($9,900) for the fountain pen and 6,850 euros ($8,250) for the rollerball, 30% to 40% of the entire Automobili Lamborghini Miura run is already pre-sold to loyal collectors reserving favorite numbers like 4, 8, 10, or 13. Backed by 35 years of stocked spare parts and custom-machined components that keep pens manufactured in 1912 writing today, a Miura pen crafted by Montegrappa "can be handed over from generation to generation," Aquila warmly concluded.
